newsitem.title: MONACO: ATHLETICS-IAAF TO PAY $10 MILLION PRIZE MONEY NEXT YEAR.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IAAF TO PAY $10 MILLION PRIZE MONEY NEXT YEAR.

text.p: Ten million dollars will be available in prize money for athletes next year, sources in the sport said on Thursday.

The figure would be announced by International Amateur Athletic Federation president Primo Nebiolo at a news conference on Friday following a two-day IAAF council meeting which concluded on Wednesday night, the sources said.
The IAAF will award prize money at next year's world indoor and outdoor championships for the first time as well as at the grand prix final scheduled for Fukuoka, Japan.
Paris will host the indoor championships and Athens will stage the outdoor version.
The sources said prize money for the grand prix final would remain the same at $3,388,000.

The IAAF's commitment to almost trebling its prize money, plus awarding cash bonuses of $100,000 for athletes setting world records in Athens, comes at a time when the federation has still to find a sponsor for its grand prix circuit.
After severing its ties with Mobil last year the IAAF paid $2 million olp support the circuit and will pay a similar amount next season.
The federation hope to announce a sponsor for the 1998 season after an extraordinary meeting of its grand prix commission next April.
The sources said the federation had been given only $8 million by the International Olympic Committee from its Atlanta revenues.
"The total value from ticket sales alone in Atlanta for athletics was $72,497,407," they said. "That does not include television rights or sponsors.
"Our athletes put on the show and the IOC get to keep the money. Our development programme alone costs $5 million a year."
At its meeting the council decided to award the 1998 grand prix final to Moscow ahead of Helsinki and Palma de Mallorca in Spain.
Japan gains another major meeting with Maebishi hosting the 1999 world indoor championships ahead of Lisbon.
The council also decided to allow decathlete Eduard Hamalainen to compete for Finland next year.
Hamalainen, who now lives in Finland, won the silver medal for Belarus at both the 1993 and 1995 world championships.
His family were originally deported from Finland to the Soviet Union during the Stalinist era.
